Juvenile Volk (Cottus volki) grow slowly in the cold streams they inhabit, ultimately attaining a maximum total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] as adults. Field surveys indicate that this ultimate length is reached only after several years of steady body growth, a pattern consistent with other benthic cottids adapted to low-productivity environments. The species exhibits a moderate size at the onset of gonadal development, with puberty occurring when individuals measure approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters] in total length, a size typically achieved during the second summer of life. Data on early life stages remain somewhat limited, but recent laboratory observations have documented that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, measured immediately after eclosion, have a wet weight of 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.63 millimeters. This modest neonatal mass reflects the small, energy-dense eggs typical of freshwater sculpins, which provide sufficient endogenous yolk reserves to sustain the prolarva through the non-feeding period before the trophic switch to exogenous feeding.

Extensive mark-recapture studies conducted in a montane tributary of the Volga River basin have yielded robust estimates of the species' longevity. The maximum lifespan recorded for Cottus volki under natural thermal conditions at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of its genus. This extended lifespan at a low temperature aligns with the general pattern observed in cold-water ectotherms, where reduced metabolic rates are associated with delayed senescence and prolonged reproductive windows. It is worth noting that captive individuals maintained at the same constant temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] have been documented to survive for up to 2,555 days [am = up to 2,555 days], which is consistent with the field-based estimate when accounting for the absence of predation and environmental stressors in aquarium settings. Such longevity, likely attributable to the reduced metabolic demands imposed by the persistently cold thermal regime, is notable for a fish of such modest body size.

The reproductive biology of Cottus volki is characterized by a single, well-defined annual spawning event. Gravid females deposit their adhesive eggs in a single nest per year [F_R_i = single nest per year], and each clutch typically contains between 150 and 250 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch typically contains between 150 and 250 eggs]. These values were obtained from dissections of ripe females collected just prior to the breeding season, with egg counts performed under a dissecting microscope. The annual reproductive output appears to be tuned to the relatively cool thermal regime of the species' habitat, which constrains the duration of the growing season available for yolk synthesis and vitellogenesis. The moderately high fecundity per clutchnan compensates for the low frequency of spawning events, ensuring that a sufficient number of offspring are produced despite the brief annual window for reproduction. The cold water temperatures limit metabolic rates and the rate of vitellogenesis, shaping this life-history strategy.

Larval development proceeds through a series of well-defined stages that are heavily influenced by ambient temperature. After the completion of yolk-sac resorption, the exogenously feeding pelagic larva enters a period of rapid growth that culminates in a pronounced larval metamorphosis. The pelvic fins and rays ossify during this transformation, and the body plan reorganizes from a fusiform, transparent larva into a benthic, pigmented juvenile. This metamorphic climax typically occurs approximately 45 days after hatching when the water temperature remains at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], though the exact timing can vary by a week or more depending on local microhabitat conditions. During the preflexion and flexion stages, the larvae rely heavily on copepod nauplii and small cladocerans as their primary prey, and the successful transition to the benthic juvenile stage is contingent upon the availability of these prey items at the time of first feeding.

The habitat preferences of Cottus volki are strongly tied to interstitial spaces within gravel and cobble substrates, where adults seek refuge from both predators and high flow events. The species is most commonly encountered in pool-riffle complexes characterized by well-oxygenated water and a stable thermal regime. Spawning occurs in late winter to early spring, with males establishing nests beneath flat stones where they guard the egg mass until eclosion. The male provides exclusive paternal care during the incubation period, fanning the eggs to ensure adequate oxygenation and removing any that become fungused. This reproductive investment, combined with the extended lifespan exceeding seven years, suggests that Cottus volki follows a relatively slow pace of life compared to other freshwater cottids, with an emphasis on adult survivorship and repeated, low-fecundity spawning events rather than a single, high-output reproductive bout.
